title: Fathers Are Not Mothers, They Are Unique and Irreplaceable
author: Lisa Britton
summary: Britton opens with a scene from a Super Bowl party, watching her boyfriend console a disappointed son, and uses it to set up a two-part argument. The first part is affirming: fathers really are more engaged than any previous generation, IFS and other data show married dads of young children doing far more child care and housework than their 1960s counterparts, and the benefits to children are documented in self-regulation, behavior, language and adolescent outcomes. The second part is her actual target, which is the way that engagement gets praised. She objects to a framing in which the highest compliment available to a father is that he parents like a mother, singling out a recent Independent piece on caring fathers as sympathetic in substance but wrong in framing, and she reads Gloria Steinem's late interview as treating baby carriers as proof that the sexes are interchangeable. Against interchangeability she argues for complementarity, claiming that families thrive on different strengths brought to shared work rather than on sameness, and that erasing the difference produces confusion and resentment rather than fairness. She extends the point to the labor market, endorsing calls for more male teachers and nurses but insisting the reason is that masculine presence belongs in those roles, not that men should imitate women in them. Her illustration of the alternative is the Brooklyn father who takes his daughter to Saturday ballet and bonds with the other dads there.
points: Britton accepts the empirical story of rising paternal involvement and then attacks the interpretive frame placed on it, which is a different move from the usual absent-father argument.
Her central objection is that treating mothering as the standard of good parenting diminishes both parents, making womanhood the default and manhood a costume.

She names specific paternal contributions she considers non-substitutable: risk-edged play, raised expectations of capability, protective presence, and an authority figure that shapes how boys later regard authority.
The ballet-class example is offered as the model, fathers giving time in a distinctly male way rather than performing a maternal role.
The argument extends into labor markets, supporting more men in teaching and nursing precisely because masculine presence, not male imitation of female norms, is what those settings lack.
quotes: Too many people today talk as if fathers are simply second mothers—as if a family is just two interchangeable adults dividing tasks on a spreadsheet.

Research shows that fathers are more engaged at home and with their children than any generation of men before them. Data from the Institute for Family Studies and other researchers finds that married dads of young children now spend far more hours on child care and housework than their counterparts did in the 1960s.

Children with married, engaged dads have stronger self-regulation, fewer behavioral problems, better language development, and a clearer path into adulthood. Boys are less likely to fall into trouble.

The more we pretend that fathers are the same as mothers, the more we damage the relationship between men and women. Families don’t thrive on sameness. They thrive on complementarity: two people bringing different strengths to the same beloved work.
She lit up describing how many men now wear baby carriers and push strollers. She treated it as proof that men are the same as women and this sameness is a great advance for society.

When we tell fathers to parent as if they were mothers, we don’t elevate fatherhood. We diminish motherhood and fatherhood. We treat womanhood as the default human setting and manhood as a costume that should be removed for the good of the children.
But the reason we need men in those professions is because masculine energy belongs there, too. A male teacher helps a restless boy by being a man the boy can watch, test himself against, and trust.
This is a great way to integrate father presence without dads pretending to be moms. They give their time in the best way, cheer on their daughters, and get to be men at the same time.
